evidence.note: The OpenAI/Hugging Face story runs at confidence "medium" on TechCrunch and Fortune alone, correctly handling a blocked primary: OpenAI's own report is quoted directly by both outlets, the story never claims high confidence, and the prose says 'per OpenAI's account as reported by both outlets' rather than citing the report itself. The lead has two genuinely independent sources including NVIDIA's own newsroom. Several standard/brief stories (Thomson Reuters, Lambda, Razorpay, Alice) rest on a single tier-2/3 source, each correctly capped at medium confidence and phrased as 'according to X' rather than presented as verified fact — sourcing that would survive a challenge but isn't uniformly two-deep.

The Razorpay story's numbers (3 trillion data points, 4 billion transactions, 8-10% success-rate lift, 8X fraud detection, 5X dispute detection) and the Harshil Mathur quote were checked directly against Inc42's article during this review pass — the draft had originally paired an AWS-press-release-only quote with Inc42-sourced figures, which would have misattributed the quote; it was replaced with the quote Inc42 itself reports. Vendor benchmark figures elsewhere (Qwen3.8-Max's Terminal-Bench/SWE-bench scores, Thomson Reuters' LegalBench score) are explicitly flagged as company-reported or single-outlet and 'not independently reproduced.'

Bullets across the edition state facts, not topics — e.g. the lead's third bullet quotes Dion Harris directly rather than summarizing vaguely. Decks add information beyond the headline throughout (the Nvidia deck names NVLink Fusion specifically; the Sony/Warner deck names the separate existing litigation). The CHIVE story's second body paragraph is a single long compound sentence carrying a quote, a method description and an attribution together — readable but a copy desk would likely split it.

The lead (Nvidia/MediaTek) is defensible on durability and materiality — it restructures a vendor relationship and Nvidia's revenue model, not just a one-time announcement — but a reasonable editor could argue the OpenAI/Hugging Face autonomous-agent breach, with a documented root-level production compromise, was the more dramatic story of the day. It was placed at 'top' rather than 'lead' in part because its best source is a blocked primary (OpenAI's own report returned 403 to direct fetch), which is exactly the case where the lead-needs-a-tier-1-primary rule and a defensible news judgment both point to the same swap, but it means the lead call is arguable rather than unanimous.

The 'infrastructure' beat carries only its lead story against a target of two, and top-prominence stories sit at 2 against a house range of 3-6 — both are advisory notes, not warnings, and the editor's note ('Elsewhere: Sony Music and Warner Chappell become the latest to sue Anthropic, Thomson Reuters bets on owning its AI rather than renting it...') does name the day's other threads rather than pretending the edition is only about the top two stories. No single company drives more than 2 of 10 stories as its actual subject (Anthropic: the Sony/Warner suit and the CHIVE paper); Nvidia appears as a named party in three stories but is only the subject of one.
